title: Why Prices Won't Stop Rising: Inflation by the Numbers
note: EP028 — explainer (By the Numbers, row 17). Inflation: CPI, the three causes, the 2021-23 surge, compounding erosion, winners/losers, shrinkflation, wage-price spiral, how it's tamed. Free memes; 5 new motifs (basketprice, demandpull, costpush, erode, shrinkflation). Target 12–15 min.

scenes.narration: Pull an old photo of a price tag — a candy bar, a gallon of gas, a house — from a few decades ago. The number looks absurd now. Impossibly cheap.
Prices, it seems, only ever go one direction: up. And not by accident. The whole system is quietly designed to make your money worth a little less every single year.
Here's the number that should stop you. A dollar from 1970 buys you roughly what fifteen cents did back then. Most of its value has simply evaporated.
You didn't lose that money in a crash. It leaked away, penny by penny, through a force most people never really understand.
So why won't prices stop rising — and who actually benefits from a system built to erode your money? Let's do it by the numbers.
Why do prices never stop climbing? Let's follow the money — upward.
scenes.heading: Why Prices Won't Stop Rising
scenes.sub: Your money is designed to lose value.

scenes.narration: Start with the word itself. Inflation is a general, sustained rise in the overall price of goods and services.
Not one thing getting pricier — everything, on average, drifting up. Which flips into a second fact: as prices rise, each dollar in your pocket buys a little less.
So how do we even measure 'prices in general'? You can't track every price on Earth. So statisticians use a clever trick: a basket.
They build a representative basket of everything a typical household buys — food, rent, gas, clothes — and track its total price over time.
That's the Consumer Price Index. Same basket, measured again and again. When the total creeps up, that percentage is your inflation rate.
scenes.caption: the same cart, ticking up

scenes.narration: That basket is imperfect, though. Economists strip out volatile food and energy to get 'core' inflation — and critics argue the official number can understate what you actually feel.
And here's the surprise: a little inflation isn't a bug. It's the target. Central banks deliberately aim for around two percent a year.
Why aim for your money to lose value? Because, as we've seen, the alternative — falling prices — is far more dangerous. A gentle, predictable rise keeps the economy moving.
Why two percent, exactly? It's a deliberate buffer — high enough to stay safely clear of dangerous deflation, low enough that people barely notice it. Close enough to invisible.
So if a little is on purpose, why does it sometimes roar out of control? There are three engines behind it.
scenes.heading: The Three Engines

scenes.narration: Engine one: demand-pull. This is when the demand for stuff outruns the supply of it.
Too much money, chasing too few goods. When everyone has cash and wants to buy, but there isn't enough to go around, sellers simply raise prices. They can.
scenes.caption: too much money, too few goods

scenes.narration: This is the 'good problem' version — a red-hot economy, everyone spending. But let it run too hot, and prices sprint away from wages.
Engine two: cost-push. Here, inflation comes from the supply side — the cost of making things jumps.
When oil, wages, or shipping get more expensive, every business that depends on them has to raise prices just to survive. The cost gets pushed up the chain, onto you.
scenes.caption: costs shove prices up from below

scenes.narration: An oil shock is the classic case. Energy touches almost everything — so when oil spikes, the price of food, plastic, travel and delivery all climb together.
Engine three is the deepest one: money itself. Print far more money than the economy produces in goods, and each unit is worth less — the oldest cause of inflation there is.
More dollars, same amount of stuff. Mathematically, the prices simply have to rise to soak up all the extra money.
scenes.caption: more money → higher prices

scenes.narration: One subtlety: printing money only ignites inflation if that money actually gets spent. Pile it in a vault and it sleeps. Push it into people's hands who spend it, and prices move.
It's never just 'they printed money.' It's printed money, meeting real demand, chasing limited goods.
Put all three engines together, and you get a storm. Which is exactly what happened in the early 2020s.
scenes.heading: The Perfect Storm

scenes.narration: First, during the pandemic, governments and central banks flooded the world with money — stimulus checks, cheap loans, and trillions in new cash. That was the fuel.
At the same time, supply chains seized up. Factories closed, ports jammed, and goods became scarce. So demand surged just as supply shrank.
A mountain of new money, chasing a shrunken pile of goods. Demand-pull and cost-push, firing at the same time. The textbook recipe for a price explosion.
scenes.caption: every engine firing at once

scenes.narration: Then energy prices spiked on top of it all. The result was the worst inflation in forty years — prices rising faster than most people alive had ever seen.
For a while, officials insisted it was 'transitory' — temporary, about to fade. It did not fade on schedule.
At its 2022 peak, US inflation hit around nine percent — the highest in four decades. In parts of the world, it ran far, far hotter.
Suddenly a word most people had filed under 'boring economics' was the thing emptying their wallet every week.
Now for the part that actually hits your wallet — because inflation isn't just a headline, it compounds.
scenes.heading: The Quiet Theft

scenes.narration: Inflation works like compound interest in reverse. Even a 'modest' three percent a year stacks, year on year, quietly eating your money's value.
Here's what that does to a hundred dollars sitting in cash. It doesn't crash. It just melts — a little more every year, until half of it is simply gone.
scenes.caption: what $100 in cash is really worth

scenes.narration: There's a handy shortcut, the rule of 72. At three percent inflation, your money loses half its value in about twenty-four years. At six percent, just twelve.
So how do you fight back? You can't stop inflation — but you can refuse to just hold cash. Owning assets that rise with prices is how people protect their money's value.
Governments even sell inflation-protected bonds whose value rises with prices, and tie some pensions to the cost of living. Little lifeboats bolted onto a sinking currency.
So cash isn't safe. Money stuffed under a mattress is guaranteed to lose purchasing power. Inflation is a slow, silent tax on everyone who holds dollars.
Which raises the real question. If someone is losing, someone is winning. So who actually benefits from inflation?
scenes.heading: Winners and Losers

scenes.narration: Loser number one: savers, and anyone holding cash. Their money quietly shrinks. Loser two: anyone on a fixed income, like a pensioner, whose payment doesn't keep up.
Loser three: workers whose wages lag behind. If prices rise five percent and your raise is two, you just took a pay cut — even though the number on your paycheck went up.
Now the winners. Winner one: borrowers. If you owe a fixed debt, inflation quietly shrinks it — you repay with dollars that are worth less than the ones you borrowed.
Which makes the biggest winner of all… the government. It's the largest borrower on Earth, and inflation quietly erodes the real value of its enormous debt.
So inflation is really a vast, invisible transfer — from savers to borrowers, from workers to asset-owners, and from citizens to the state. All without a single vote.
scenes.caption: a silent wealth transfer

scenes.narration: Notice the quiet conflict of interest. The institution measuring and 'fighting' inflation — the government — is also its single biggest beneficiary. Mild inflation erodes its mountain of debt.
Winner two: owners of real assets. Houses, stocks, gold — their prices tend to rise with inflation. So those who own things pull away from those who just hold cash.
And some of inflation is deliberately hidden from you — right on the supermarket shelf.
scenes.heading: The Hidden Kind

scenes.narration: The sneakiest trick has a name: shrinkflation. Instead of raising the price, they quietly shrink the product.
The chip bag costs the same four dollars — but now it's got a little less in it. The price held; the value didn't. It's a price hike you're not supposed to notice.
scenes.caption: same price, less product

scenes.narration: Watch for its cousins too: the candy bar that's thinner, the roll with fewer sheets, the 'new recipe' made with cheaper ingredients. All inflation, wearing a disguise.
Which is why the official rate and your lived experience can feel like two different planets.
scenes.memeBottom: the real rise you feel at the store

scenes.narration: Here's the scariest part: inflation can feed on itself, through pure psychology.
scenes.heading: The Spiral

scenes.narration: The classic version is the wage-price spiral — where rising wages and rising prices chase each other upward.
Workers see prices rising, so they demand higher wages. Companies pay them, then raise prices to cover it. Which makes workers demand even higher wages. Round and round.
Underneath it all is expectation. If everyone simply believes prices will keep rising, they act in ways that make it come true. Inflation becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Let it run unchecked and you reach the nightmare end state — hyperinflation, where money loses value by the day.
That's why central banks guard expectations so fiercely. Once people stop believing prices are under control, inflation gets wildly harder to stop.
History shows it CAN be beaten — brutally. In the early 1980s, US inflation was raging, and the Fed's Paul Volcker jacked interest rates up toward twenty percent to break it.
It worked — but it triggered a savage recession, with unemployment spiking. The cure for runaway inflation is a dose of economic pain severe enough to scare it back down.
So how do you actually kill high inflation? With a blunt, painful instrument.
scenes.heading: How It's Tamed

scenes.narration: The central bank raises interest rates. Suddenly borrowing is expensive, so people and businesses borrow and spend less. Demand cools — and prices stop sprinting.
But that cure has a side effect. Choke demand hard enough and you can choke the whole economy — fewer sales, fewer jobs, a recession. The medicine can be brutal.
It's a tightrope. Too little, and inflation runs wild. Too much, and you trigger a downturn. Central bankers spend their whole careers trying to land exactly in the middle.
And here's a final twist that confuses almost everyone. When inflation 'falls,' prices usually don't. They just rise more slowly.
That's disinflation — the rate slowing down. It is not deflation, which is prices actually falling. The high prices you're angry about mostly stay. They just stop climbing so fast.
scenes.caption: the rate slows — the prices stay

scenes.narration: This is why, even after inflation 'cools,' everything still feels expensive. The prices never came back down. They just caught their breath.
Over time, wages do slowly catch up — through raises, and cost-of-living adjustments tied to the index. But they usually lag, so you feel poorer on the way up.
The prices jump the moment there's an excuse. Your pay negotiates, waits, and limps along behind.
So let's add up the receipts on inflation.
scenes.heading: The Takeaway

scenes.narration: A little inflation is the plan. Too much money or too few goods lets it roar. It compounds, quietly halving your cash. And it hits savers hardest, while rewarding debtors.
Inflation isn't random bad luck. It's a force baked into the system — useful in small doses, devastating in large ones, and always, quietly, moving wealth around.
So the single most useful takeaway is almost rude in its simplicity. In an inflationary world, holding pure cash is a slow guaranteed loss — and owning productive assets is the defense.
Inflation punishes the saver who does nothing and quietly rewards the one who owns a piece of the economy.
scenes.memeBottom: owning a slice of the economy

scenes.narration: Which is the real lesson. Inflation is a tax nobody voted for — paid automatically by everyone holding cash, collected by everyone holding debt and assets.
So the next time prices climb and the headline says inflation is 'only' three percent, you'll know what that number is quietly doing to the money in your account.
